subject: how to produce a multiple plots comparing two groups, one for each of several variables vs time

messages.author: 561b723b7d8f7401
messages.subject: how to produce a multiple plots comparing two groups, one for each of several variables vs time
parts:
Hi, new to ggplot, so am just getting my head around how it works, and am hoping for some help in pointing me in the right direction.

Suppose I have the following data:

> test.df
  ID group          X           Y          Z time
1  1     A -0.2300575  0.59433108  0.7463163    1
2  2     B -0.8592283 -0.04834775 -0.3927258    1
3  3     C  0.5961568  0.13914823  0.6158333    1
4  1     A  0.4895552 -0.10457984 -1.2070888    2
5  2     B  1.8303039 -0.06716994  0.1888753    2
6  3     C  0.6726456 -1.58981685  1.7563034    2

I know I can use facet_grid to produce, say, a plot that contains a graph of X vs time for each group:

> ggplot(test.df, aes(x=factor(time), y=X, group=ID)) + facet_grid(. ~ group) + geom_line()

However, I don't see how to produce a plot that contains, for each group in {A,B} and for each variable in {X,Y}, a graph of V vs time; e.g., a plot of the form

  X v time (A)   ||   X v time (B)
  Y v time (A)   ||   Y v time (B)

Thanks in advance for you any guidance you can provide!

Cheers,
David Romano

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: how to produce a multiple plots comparing two groups, one for each of several variables vs time
parts:
Hi:

I'm not exactly sure that I interpreted your request correctly, but
here's one shot at it.

# Read in the data
test.df <- structure(list(ID = c(1L, 2L, 3L, 1L, 2L, 3L), group =
structure(c(1L,
2L, 3L, 1L, 2L, 3L), .Label = c("A", "B", "C"), class = "factor"),
X = c(-0.2300575, -0.8592283, 0.5961568, 0.4895552, 1.8303039,
0.6726456), Y = c(0.59433108, -0.04834775, 0.13914823, -0.10457984,
-0.06716994, -1.58981685), Z = c(0.7463163, -0.3927258, 0.6158333,
-1.2070888, 0.1888753, 1.7563034), time = c(1L, 1L, 1L, 2L,
2L, 2L)), .Names = c("ID", "group", "X", "Y", "Z", "time"
), class = "data.frame", row.names = c("1", "2", "3", "4", "5",
"6"))

library(ggplot2)

# Plot X and Y separately over time by group
ggplot(subset(test.df, group != "C"), aes(x = factor(time), y = X,
color = group)) +
geom_point(size = 3) + xlab("time")

ggplot(subset(test.df, group != "C"), aes(x = factor(time), y = Y,
color = group)) +
geom_point(size = 3) + labs(x = "time")

# Add lines to the plot
ggplot(subset(test.df, group != "C"), aes(x = factor(time), y = X,
color = group)) +
geom_point(size = 3) +
geom_line(aes(group = group), size = 1) + xlab("time")

ggplot(subset(test.df, group != "C"), aes(x = factor(time), y = Y,
color = group)) +
geom_point(size = 3) +
geom_line(aes(group = group), size = 1) + xlab("time")


A few comments:

1. It worked this time, but it is usually a bad idea to copy and paste
data from the R console into an e-mail. It's better to call the dput()
function and copy/paste the output from that:

> dput(test.df)
structure(list(ID = c(1L, 2L, 3L, 1L, 2L, 3L), group = structure(c(1L,
2L, 3L, 1L, 2L, 3L), .Label = c("A", "B", "C"), class = "factor"),
X = c(-0.2300575, -0.8592283, 0.5961568, 0.4895552, 1.8303039,
0.6726456), Y = c(0.59433108, -0.04834775, 0.13914823, -0.10457984,
-0.06716994, -1.58981685), Z = c(0.7463163, -0.3927258, 0.6158333,
-1.2070888, 0.1888753, 1.7563034), time = c(1L, 1L, 1L, 2L,
2L, 2L)), .Names = c("ID", "group", "X", "Y", "Z", "time"
), class = "data.frame", row.names = c("1", "2", "3", "4", "5",
"6"))

dput() outputs a textual representation of the structure of an R
object. It guarantees that anyone who pops it into her R session will
see the same object you do. Moreover, it avoids formatting issues when
copying from another application such as Excel or Word. Why is dput()
good? Because anyone can copy/paste the above version of test.df into
an R session and see the same structure I sent:

> str(test.df)
'data.frame': 6 obs. of 6 variables:
$ ID : int 1 2 3 1 2 3
$ group: Factor w/ 3 levels "A","B","C": 1 2 3 1 2 3
$ X : num -0.23 -0.859 0.596 0.49 1.83 ...
$ Y : num 0.5943 -0.0483 0.1391 -0.1046 -0.0672 ...
$ Z : num 0.746 -0.393 0.616 -1.207 0.189 ...
$ time : int 1 1 1 2 2 2

If the data object is large, one can put it in Dropbox or some on-line
data repository that people can download from an URL into R (not
necessarily in dput form, but one that R can input easily).

2. More specific to the plots above, when the x-variable is a factor,
geom_line() or geom_path() won't render unless you have mapped a group
aesthetic. Notice that one can map aesthetics within a geom call, in
which case the mapping is local to the geom. When aesthetics are
mapped in ggplot(), it is assumed that they are 'global' - i.e., to be
available in _every_ subsequent geom/stat call. This is one of the
first lessons that a new user of ggplot2 needs to know - the
distinction between setting an aesthetic to a constant value or
mapping it to a variable. Mappings always take place within aes();
setting of aesthetics always takes place outside of aes(). For
example, in geom_point(), the point size was set to 3 and in
geom_line, the size (line thickness) was set to 1.

I hope this is a correct interpretation of your question.

Dennis

messages.author: 60332ae9970bf92f
messages.subject: Re: how to produce a multiple plots comparing two groups, one for each of several variables vs time
parts:
Thanks, Dennis!  Just knowing that 'subset' can be used in this way is already very helpful, and your additional comments help to shed light on aspects of ggplot usage I wasn't aware of.

What I had in mind was a two-dimensional version of the output from the command:
ggplot(subset(test.df, group!="C"), aes(x=factor(time), y=X, group=ID)) + facet_grid(. ~ group) + geom_line()

So the output would be a multiplot array of dimension (# of selected variables) by (# of selected groups).

I wasn't sure if a loop would be necessary when the size of the selections were big enough, or whether ggplot might already allow for using subsets of (y-)variables together with subsets of the collection of groups as input, so that the output is a matrix of plots.

Thanks again,
David
